sentences.text: Opisthocoelicaudia was a relatively small sauropod measuring between 11.4 and 13 meters in length from head to tail tip.
Studies have estimated the body mass of this dinosaur at various figures, including 8.4, 10.5, 13, 22, and 25.4 tonnes.
The name Opisthocoelicaudia means "posterior cavity tail" or "posteriorly excavated tail," referring to the concave posterior sides of its anterior tail vertebrae.
Only two additional, incomplete specimens are known, consisting of a shoulder fragment and a tail fragment.
The best-preserved Opisthocoelicaudia footprint measures 63 cm across, suggesting it was made by an individual larger than the known type specimen.
A preserved skin impression above a toe print shows non-overlapping scales with an average diameter of 14 mm.
In 2017, researchers described a kidney-shaped sauropod forefoot impression, the first of its kind found in the Nemegt Formation.
A nearly complete skeleton of Opisthocoelicaudia was discovered in 1965 by Polish and Mongolian scientists, which lacks only the head.
The type specimen was found between June 10 and 23, 1965, during an expedition led by paleontologist Zofia Kielan-Jaworowska.
Recent studies suggest Opisthocoelicaudia carried its neck relatively straight and horizontally, contrary to earlier S-curved reconstructions.
A 2007 study by Schwarz and colleagues proposed that Opisthocoelicaudia's back dipped towards the rear.
Researchers propose that Opisthocoelicaudia could rear up on its hind legs based on its skeletal features, potentially using its tail as a third leg for foraging.
In 2011, Heinrich Mallison hypothesized that Opisthocoelicaudia could angle its tail to create a midsection buckle during rearing.
Bite marks on the pelvis and thigh bone indicate that predators fed on the carcass and likely removed the missing parts.
The genus Opisthocoelicaudia was established by Borsuk-Bialynicka in 1977.
Opisthocoelicaudia was originally classified within the family Camarasauridae alongside Camarasaurus and Euhelopus, but is now considered a derived member of Titanosauria.
Currently, Opisthocoelicaudia is classified within the superfamily Titanosauria.
Opisthocoelicaudia lived during the Late Cretaceous Period in the Gobi Desert of Mongolia.
The fossils come from the Nemegt Formation, which was deposited during the Late Cretaceous but has never been radiometrically dated.
Scientists estimate the Nemegt Formation dates to between the late Campanian and middle Maastrichtian stages, specifically from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
It is debated whether Nemegtosaurus and Opisthocoelicaudia represent the same species due to the lack of a known skull for Opisthocoelicaudia, a view suggested by Jeffrey Wilson in 2005.
It is also debated whether Opisthocoelicaudia and Alamosaurus form a monophyletic group called Opisthocoelicaudiinae or if that group is paraphyletic.
